It's valid because the conclusion turned out to be true
It's valid because it uses the word 'therefore'
items.explanation: Validity is a purely structural test: does the conclusion have to follow if the premises are granted? Here it does — nothing about whether the sign is actually accurate changes whether the structure forces the conclusion from the premises.
items.reference:
Premises true
Structure valid
Sound

Why: validity only asks whether the conclusion is forced by the premises — it never asks whether the premises are actually true.
items.learnMore:
Validity vs. truth

An argument is valid if there is no possible case where all its premises are true and its conclusion is false. This is checkable with premises that are obviously false in reality — "all cats are reptiles; Fido is a cat; therefore Fido is a reptile" is valid, because the conclusion really is forced if you grant those premises, even though every claim in it is false.

QuestionAnswers
Is it valid?Does the conclusion have to follow, granting the premises?
Is it sound?Is it valid AND are the premises actually true?

Common mistake

Calling an argument invalid because a premise is false, or because the conclusion feels wrong. Both of those are about soundness or truth, not validity.

items.explanation: This generalizes from three specific observations to a claim about Mondays in general. It doesn't claim certainty — it claims a probable pattern, which is exactly what makes it inductive rather than deductive.

items.prompt: What does formal logic study, as distinct from informal logic?
choices: Formal logic studies only mathematics, informal logic studies only everyday speech

Formal logic studies argument structure independent of content — the same pattern is valid or invalid no matter what real claims fill it in; informal logic studies arguments as they actually occur in language, including ambiguity and unstated assumptions
Formal logic is for professionals, informal logic is for casual conversation
There's no real distinction — they're two names for the same field
items.explanation: Formal logic evaluates the shape of an argument abstractly — "if P then Q; P; therefore Q" is valid no matter what P and Q stand for. Informal logic deals with real language, where ambiguity, tone, and unstated assumptions matter and formal notation isn't explicitly written out.
items.reference:
Formal

Structure, independent of content

Informal

Real language: ambiguity, unstated assumptions

Why: "closed every Monday" vs. "closed most Mondays" is exactly the kind of ambiguity formal structure alone doesn't catch.
items.learnMore:
Same argument, two lenses

Formal logic could confirm that "if open, lights on; lights on; therefore open" is invalid (affirming the consequent), purely from its shape. It can't tell you whether a real speaker meant "open implies lights on" as a strict rule or a rough tendency — that's an informal-logic question about how the claim was actually phrased and intended.

Common mistake

Treating informal logic as "less rigorous." It's a different, complementary discipline — necessary because most real arguments never get formal notation written out.

items.prompt: "If the bakery is open, the lights are on. The bakery is open. Therefore the lights are on." What pattern is this, and is it valid?
choices: Affirming the consequent — invalid
Modus ponens — valid in every case, regardless of what the two claims actually are
Denying the antecedent — invalid
This can't be evaluated without checking if the lights are actually on
items.explanation: This is "if P then Q; P; therefore Q" — modus ponens, valid no matter what real-world claims fill in P and Q. Granting both premises forces the conclusion.
items.reference:
NameAdded factValid?
Modus ponensOpenYes
Modus tollensLights not onYes
Affirming consequentLights onNo
Denying antecedentNot openNo

Why: the house rule ("open implies lights on") only licenses two of these four moves.
items.learnMore:
Why modus ponens always works

If "if P then Q" is granted as true, and P is also granted as true, there is no possible world where Q fails — that's exactly what "if P then Q" means. This holds for any P and Q whatsoever: "if it's raining, the ground is wet; it's raining; therefore the ground is wet" has the identical structure and the identical guarantee.

Common mistake

Confusing modus ponens with affirming the consequent because both start from the same "if P then Q" premise. The direction of the second premise is what decides validity.

items.prompt: "If the bakery is open, the lights are on. The lights are on. Therefore it's open." What's wrong with this?
choices: Nothing — this is a valid modus ponens argument
It affirms the consequent — the house rule only says open implies lights-on, not the reverse, so the lights being on doesn't rule out other reasons (like a cleaning crew) for them being on

items.explanation: The rule promises only one direction: open implies lights-on. Lights-on doesn't logically rule out other causes (a cleaning crew arriving early), so "lights on, therefore open" isn't forced by the premises — it's invalid, specifically affirming the consequent.
items.reference:
📋 Rule: open → lights on (one direction only)
💡 Observed: lights on
❌ Claimed: therefore open — NOT forced
🧹 Counterexample: cleaning crew, lights on, not open

Why: the rule never claimed lights-on happens ONLY when open — that extra assumption was smuggled in.
items.learnMore:
The missing assumption

"If P then Q" only guarantees Q when P holds — it says nothing about what else might also produce Q. Affirming the consequent quietly assumes an extra, unstated premise: "Q happens only when P." Without that stronger premise being separately established, "Q, therefore P" isn't forced.

Stated ruleWhat it does NOT claim
Open → lights onLights on → open

Common mistake

Assuming an "if P then Q" rule works in both directions. It never does unless separately stated as an "if and only if."

items.prompt: "If the bakery is open, the lights are on. The lights are not on. Therefore it's not open." Is this valid?
choices: No — this denies the antecedent
Yes — this is modus tollens: if being open guarantees lights-on, then lights being off rules out being open entirely, since there'd be no way to be open with the lights off
No — the lights could be broken instead
Only valid if you also confirm the door is locked
items.explanation: This is "if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P" — modus tollens. Since the rule guarantees lights-on whenever open, the absence of lights-on rules out being open, with no exceptions the rule allows for.
items.reference:

↓
Lights NOT on
↓ no way to be open with lights off

Why: denying the consequent ("not Q") rules out the antecedent ("P") completely, given the rule.
items.learnMore:
Why modus tollens is the mirror image of affirming the consequent

"If P then Q" guarantees Q whenever P holds. So if Q is absent, P can't have held either — otherwise Q would be guaranteed, contradicting its absence. This works precisely because the rule is a one-way guarantee, the same one-way guarantee that makes affirming the consequent (arguing from Q's presence to P) invalid.

Common mistake

Confusing modus tollens (reasoning from Q's absence) with affirming the consequent (reasoning from Q's presence) — they look similar but only one is valid.

"If P then Q" says nothing whatsoever about what happens when P is false. Q could still hold (via some other cause) or not — the rule simply doesn't cover that case. Denying the antecedent treats the rule as if it also said "if not P, then not Q," which was never claimed.

Common mistake

Reading "if P then Q" as also implying "if not P then not Q." A rule about one direction says nothing about its opposite.

items.prompt: Per L2's confidence chart, what happens to confidence in "it's closed on Mondays" as more consistent Mondays are checked?
choices: It stays exactly the same regardless of evidence
It climbs quickly at first, then flattens out — approaching but never reaching 100% certainty
It reaches 100% once you've checked at least ten Mondays
It decreases, because more checking increases the chance of eventually finding an exception
items.explanation: The chart's curve rises fast with early evidence, then flattens — each additional consistent check adds less new confidence than the last, and the curve approaches 100% without ever touching it. That gap between "very confident" and "certain" is the deductive/inductive divide.
items.reference:
📈 More consistent evidence → higher confidence
🚧 Curve flattens, never reaches 100%
🎯 Deductive certainty is the only way to actually reach 100%

Why: inductive strength grows with evidence but never converts into a deductive guarantee.
items.learnMore:
Strong evidence is not the same as proof

Ten consistent Mondays make "closed on Mondays" a very good bet — clearly stronger than three. But no finite number of consistent observations logically rules out an exception on the next one, the way a valid deductive argument's premises rule out its conclusion being false. That's not a flaw in the reasoning; it's the actual, honest nature of inductive evidence.

Common mistake

Treating "we've checked a lot" as equivalent to "we've proven it." Strong inductive evidence still isn't a deductive guarantee, no matter how much of it there is.

Because you need at least 100 observations before an argument counts as valid
Inductive arguments can never become stronger with evidence
items.explanation: Validity is a yes/no structural property of deductive arguments. Inductive arguments were never making that kind of claim to begin with — evidence moves the probability needle, but no amount of it converts a probability claim into the different category of a deductive guarantee.

items.prompt: L3's `isValid` checker found `{ valid: false, counterexample: { Open: false, LightsOn: true } }` for Priya's argument. What does that counterexample actually mean?
choices: That the bakery was definitely closed that day
That there exists a possible situation (closed, but lights on) where both premises hold and the conclusion fails — exactly the scenario a cleaning crew creates
That the checker made an error and should be re-run
That the argument is valid after all, since a counterexample was found
items.explanation: A counterexample is a concrete assignment where the premises are true but the conclusion is false — proof the structure doesn't force the conclusion. `Open: false, LightsOn: true` is precisely the cleaning-crew case: lights on, not actually open.
items.reference:
Try all combinations of Open, LightsOn
↓
Found: Open=false, LightsOn=true — premises hold, conclusion fails
↓
Verdict: invalid

Why: a single counterexample is enough to prove an argument invalid — that's the whole mechanism the brute-force checker relies on.
items.learnMore:
Reading a counterexample

The checker tries every combination of true/false for each variable. The moment it finds one where every premise evaluates true but the conclusion evaluates false, it stops and reports that combination — that's sufficient to prove invalidity, because validity requires the conclusion to hold in every single case, with no exceptions at all.

Common mistake

Reading a returned counterexample as a bug or a fluke. It's the entire point of the check — proof by concrete example that the structure doesn't force the conclusion.

items.prompt: In L3's conversation, Priya's conclusion ("it's open") turned out to be TRUE — the door really was unlocked. What does that tell us about her argument?
choices: That her argument was valid after all, since the conclusion was correct

Nothing about its validity — a true conclusion doesn't retroactively fix an invalid structure; she got the right answer by luck (a cleaning crew happened to be there), not because the reasoning forced it
That her argument was sound, since sound arguments always have true conclusions
That the checker's earlier verdict must have been wrong
items.explanation: Validity is about the structure, evaluated independent of any one outcome. Priya's argument (lights on, therefore open) was invalid regardless of what actually happened that day — it just happened to land on a true conclusion this time, which the next cleaning-crew-only visit wouldn't repeat.
items.reference:
💡 Priya: "lights on, so open" — invalid structure
✅ Turned out to be true this time (cleaning crew + early open)
🎲 True conclusion this time ≠ valid argument

Why: an invalid argument can still land on a true conclusion by coincidence — that doesn't make the reasoning trustworthy next time.
items.learnMore:
Lucky conclusions vs. trustworthy reasoning

An invalid argument's conclusion can still be true — the structure just doesn't guarantee it. That's the real danger of relying on invalid reasoning: it works often enough by coincidence to feel reliable, right up until the case where it isn't (the cleaning crew arrives on a day the bakery genuinely stays closed).

Common mistake

Judging an argument's validity by whether its conclusion happened to be right. Validity is evaluated on the structure, not the outcome of one instance.

items.explanation: "Invalid" is a precise, technical claim about structure — it says nothing about the speaker's competence, honesty, or intent. L3 explicitly separates the structural verdict from any judgment about Priya herself.

Naming the gap, not attacking the person

"That's invalid" said alone can land as an insult. "This affirms the consequent — lights on doesn't rule out the cleaning crew" is the actually useful version: specific, checkable, and focused on the structure rather than the person who made the argument.

items.prompt: L3 says Marcus's claim "doesn't even make sense" to run through the boolean truth-table checker. Why not?
choices: Because the checker only works with two variables, and Marcus's claim has three
Because inductive strength is a matter of degree, not a boolean fact — there's no fixed rule-shaped premise to encode the way there is for the deductive lights/open claim
Because Marcus's claim is actually deductive and the checker has a bug
Because JavaScript can't represent probabilities
items.explanation: The checker evaluates boolean premises against a boolean conclusion. Marcus's claim isn't a fixed rule plus a fact — it's a probabilistic generalization from cases, which has no boolean premise to encode. That's a real boundary of what deductive validity checking can evaluate, not a limitation specific to this particular script.
items.reference:
✅ Deductive claims: boolean premises → checker applies
❌ Inductive claims: strength is a matter of degree → checker doesn't apply
⚠️ Running the checker on Marcus's claim would be a category mistake

Why: a validity checker can only ever answer a validity question — it has nothing to say about inductive strength.
items.learnMore:
Two different tools for two different questions

"Is this deductively valid" and "how strong is this inductive evidence" are different questions requiring different kinds of scrutiny. Demanding a validity checker's yes/no verdict on an inductive claim, or demanding a probability estimate for a deductive one, both misapply the tool to the wrong kind of question.

Common mistake

Assuming any argument can be run through a validity checker if you just try hard enough. Inductive claims aren't boolean-shaped in the first place.

A validity checker answers "does this structure force a boolean conclusion" — asking it to evaluate inductive strength applies a certainty-question tool to a probability question, which is a mismatch, not a code bug.

items.prompt: Implement `isValid(variableNames, premises, conclusion)`, matching L3's brute-force truth-table checker. It should try every combination of true/false across `variableNames`, and return `{ valid: false, counterexample }` for the first assignment where every premise function returns true but the conclusion function returns false, otherwise `{ valid: true }`. Each premise/conclusion function receives an object like `{ P: true, Q: false }`.

tests.description: modus ponens (if P then Q; P; therefore Q) is valid
tests.expr: expect(isValid(['P','Q'], [(e) => !e.P || e.Q, (e) => e.P], (e) => e.Q)).toEqual({ valid: true })

tests.description: affirming the consequent (if P then Q; Q; therefore P) is invalid
affirming the consequent's counterexample has P false and Q true
tests.expr: expect(isValid(['P','Q'], [(e) => !e.P || e.Q, (e) => e.Q], (e) => e.P).counterexample).toEqual({ P: false, Q: true })

tests.description: modus tollens (if P then Q; not Q; therefore not P) is valid
denying the antecedent (if P then Q; not P; therefore not Q) is invalid

items.explanation: Validity means "no case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails" — for a fixed, small number of boolean variables that's directly checkable by trying every combination, which is exactly what the bit-counting loop does: each value of `bits` from 0 to 2^n - 1 represents one unique combination of true/false across all the variables.
items.reference:
🔢 n variables → 2^n combinations to check
🔁 bits 0 to 2^n - 1, each bit picks true/false for one variable
🛑 Stop at the first premises-true, conclusion-false case

Why: reading off each bit of a counter is a compact way to enumerate every true/false combination without writing nested loops per variable.
items.learnMore:
Why 2^n combinations

Each of the n variables independently can be true or false, so the total number of combinations is 2 multiplied by itself n times: 2^n. For 2 variables that's 4 combinations (as used by hand in the L1/L2 exercises), for 3 it's 8, and so on — brute force is only practical because logic arguments typically involve a handful of variables, not because it scales to arbitrarily large ones.

Common mistake

Forgetting to check ALL premises are true, not just the first one — an argument with multiple premises requires every one of them to hold before the conclusion is even being tested.
